1.c4 e5 2.Nc3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Sicilian
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight toward d5 and e4, so that knight and c-pawn together control d5. White keeps the centre under pressure from the flank and can still choose between a slow, closed set-up and a more active one. The cost is commitment: ...Bb4 threatens to take the knight and double White's c-pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which bears on d5 and b7 along the long diagonal, and leaves both knights uncommitted. Holding back Nc3 gives an early ...Bb4 no knight to hit, so White can choose the knights' squares later according to Black's set-up. The price is that d5 is less well covered, so ...d5 is easier for Black.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Nimzowitsch Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks e5 at once, so Black must defend the pawn or advance it. Advancing it with ...e4 kicks the knight away but leaves the pawn as a target, a sort of Alekhine's Defence with the colours reversed. White gets quick, natural development and keeps many set-ups available, while the e5-pawn ties Black to a decision.

1.c4 e5 2.a3.strategy: Prevents ...Bb4 and prepares b4 to gain queenside space, but develops nothing and adds nothing to the fight for the centre. Black can develop at leisure, so the move is sound but slow.

1.c4 e5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 to pressure e5 along the long diagonal and keeps the choice of the other set-up moves open. Black holds e5 easily and develops, so the bishop gains little at first. Sound, but slower than the main moves.

1.c4 e5 2.d3.strategy: Supports a later e4 and opens the c1-bishop for a quiet set-up. It neither develops a piece nor adds pressure on d5, so Black develops freely and prepares ...d5. Sound, but passive.

1.c4 e5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and prepares d4 to challenge e5. It does nothing against ...d5, which Black can prepare comfortably. Sound, but modest.

1.c4 e5 2.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once and opens the centre. After 2...exd4 White has to recapture with the queen, which can be chased, or first play Nf3 and take back later, and Black develops freely. White's opening edge is gone, though the game stays balanced.

1.c4 e5 2.e4.strategy: Sets up the c4 and e4 pawn pair, which clamps d5. The cost is d4, which no white pawn can cover any more, and Black aims pieces at it while ...Nf6 hits e4. Sound, but it offers White no more than the main moves.

1.c4 e5 2.Qc2.strategy: Brings the queen out before the minor pieces to cover c4 and eye e4. After ...Nc6 the knight can jump to d4 or b4 and hit the queen with tempo, while White's development lags.

1.c4 e5 2.a4.strategy: Covers b5 but develops nothing and gives up b4 for good: with the a-pawn on a4 and the c-pawn on c4, no white pawn can ever cover the square. Black can put a bishop or a knight there and develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.f3.strategy: Takes f3 from the g1-knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal, so ...Qh4+ forces g3. It covers e4 but develops nothing, and Black develops and takes the centre at leisure.

1.c4 e5 2.h3.strategy: A waiting move that loses a tempo: it prevents ...Bg4 but neither develops a piece nor contests the centre, so Black has a free hand.

1.c4 e5 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rim and weakens g4 without helping the centre or development, so Black develops and takes space with ...d5.

1.c4 e5 2.Na3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, heading for c2 or b5, and allows 2...Bxa3 3.bxa3, which leaves White with doubled, isolated a-pawns in return for the bishop pair. Otherwise the knight stands far from d5 and e4, and Black develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 or g5, but for now the e5-pawn covers f4 and the d8-queen covers g5, so the knight has no way forward from the rim. Black develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Qb3.strategy: Hits b7, which the c8-bishop guards, and brings the queen out early. 2...Nc6 followed by ...Nd4 chases it away with tempo, and White has lost time.

1.c4 e5 2.Qa4.strategy: Pins the d7-pawn against the king for a moment, but Black simply blocks the diagonal and takes the centre. The queen achieves nothing else on a4 and has spent a tempo that White's undeveloped pieces need.

1.c4 e5 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn: after 2...Bxb4 3.Bb2 the bishop hits e5, but Black holds the pawn without trouble. With the c-pawn already on c4, c3 is not available to chase the bishop, and Black stays a clean pawn up.

1.c4 e5 2.f4.strategy: Unlike the King's Gambit, it has no pawn on e4 to take over the centre: 2...exf4 simply wins a pawn and opens the e1–h4 diagonal against White's king. White must spend a tempo on Nf3 to stop ...Qh4+ before trying to win the pawn back.

1.c4 e5 2.g4.strategy: Leaves the g4-pawn without a defender and weakens f3 and h3. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop attacks g4, and 3.cxd5 Qxd5 also hits the h1-rook along the opened long diagonal.

1.c4 e5 2.c5.strategy: Pushes the c-pawn to a square where nothing defends it, and 2...Bxc5 wins it while developing the bishop toward f2. White has nothing to show for the pawn.

1.c4 e5.name: English Opening: King's English Variation
1.c4 e5.background: Also called the Reversed Sicilian, because it is a Sicilian Defence with the colours reversed; Kasparov and Keene's Batsford Chess Openings (1982) calls it the King's English. In Modern Chess Openings (14th edition, 1999), Bruce Leverett wrote that it is natural to treat the English as a Sicilian reversed, but that the results are often surprising.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Two Knights Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and takes control of d5 and e4, so White cannot build a broad centre unopposed. Black commits to no pawn structure yet and keeps every set-up open. The price is that White, with the extra tempo of a reversed Sicilian, still decides what kind of game this becomes.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Closed Sicilian
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight, guards e5 and eyes d4. Black heads for a closed game: White tends to expand on the queenside, while Black seeks counterplay with kingside pawn advances that can put White's king under pressure. It keeps the bishop and the f-pawn flexible, at the cost of a slower fight for d5.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Kramnik-Shirov Counterattack
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4.background: Popularised by Vladimir Kramnik and Alexei Shirov, who played the opening in slightly different ways.
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Attacks the c3-knight and threatens to take it, which would damage White's pawn structure. The bishop commits early and can be chased, so the game stays unclear and unbalanced. Black accepts a double-edged fight for the chance to unsettle White's queenside pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, aiming for a compact set-up with natural development. The pawn on d6 hems in the f8-bishop, and ...d5 now needs a second move, so White keeps more space in the centre. Sound, but passive.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop towards f2 but leaves e5 without a defender, so 3.Nf3 makes Black spend the next move defending it. After 3...Nc6 the fork trick 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 wins the piece back and leaves White with the bishop pair. Playable, but White has the easier game.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Be7.strategy: Prepares castling, but the bishop is passive on e7 and does not guard e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once, so Black must still spend a move defending it. Sound enough, yet White keeps the extra tempo and the easier development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Ne7.strategy: Supports a later ...d5 and leaves c6 free for the other knight, but on e7 the knight blocks the f8-bishop and does not guard e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once. Sound, yet more passive than ...Nf6, and White develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, which guards e5 and works along the long diagonal, but until the bishop arrives the h8-rook stands exposed on that diagonal. 3.d4 strikes at e5 at once, and after 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 the queen hits the rook, so Black must answer that threat at once. Playable, but less flexible than developing a knight first.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts a knight on the rim and aims for ...Nc5, but it does not defend e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once. Black must spend a further tempo while the knight is far from the action.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qe7.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the f8-bishop, and 3.Nd5 attacks the queen while also threatening Nxc7+. The queen has to move again to a square that guards c7, and White gains time.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the g8-knight. 3.Nd5 attacks it and threatens Nxc7+, so the queen has to move again to a square that guards c7, such as d8 or d6, and White gains time.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qg5.strategy: Brings the queen out early to a square where it is easily chased. 3.d4 attacks e5 and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against the queen, so 3...exd4 loses it to 4.Bxg5, and the queen must move again while White gains central space.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qh4.strategy: Brings the queen out early and hits the unprotected c4-pawn along the fourth rank. 3.Nf3 attacks the queen with tempo, and 3...Qxc4 4.Nxe5 wins the pawn back while hitting the queen again, so White gains time for development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bd6.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the d-pawn, so neither ...d6 nor ...d5 is possible and the c8-bishop stays shut in. The bishop is also a target for 3.Nb5, which threatens to take it and double Black's d-pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it guards f7 and eyes f5 but fights for no central square. Once the d-pawn moves, Bxh6 forces gxh6 and wrecks the kingside pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that guards b5 but develops nothing. 3.Nf3 attacks e5 and White gains a tempo.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Takes queenside space and prevents b4, but develops nothing, and the a-pawn can no longer cover b5, a square for White's knight. 3.Nf3 attacks e5 and White gains a tempo.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 along the long diagonal, but e5 is left to be attacked by 3.Nf3 and the bishop does not defend it. The move is slow and weakens c6.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, but takes c6 from the b8-knight and leaves e5 unguarded, so 3.Nf3 attacks it at once. Black then spends the next move on the e5-pawn instead of developing a piece.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Takes queenside space, but with pawns on c5 and e5 no black pawn can cover d5, which becomes an outpost for a white knight. It also leaves e5 loose to 3.Nf3 and develops nothing.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Offers a pawn to open the centre: 3.cxd5 Nf6 4.Nf3 Nxd5 5.Nxe5 leaves White a clean pawn up, since e5 has no defender. Black gets some activity, but too little for the pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn but takes f6 from the g8-knight, weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal and develops nothing. White builds the centre at leisure and Black's king is left exposed.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Stakes a claim on e4 but weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal before a single piece is developed. 3.d4 strikes at e5 at once, and after 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5.Qe3+ the open e-file points at the uncastled king.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that covers g5 but develops nothing and does not guard e5. 3.Nf3 attacks e5 and gains a tempo.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Starts a kingside advance without purpose and weakens g5 and g6. It develops nothing, and 3.Nf3 attacks e5 with tempo.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and blocks the f8-bishop and the queen's diagonal. The king is stuck in the centre where d4 can open the position, and nothing is gained for it.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.bxa3 simply wins a piece, and Black gets nothing in return.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn with no follow-up: 3.cxb5 simply wins it, and Black has no lead in development to make up for the pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside while e5 is undefended. 3.d4 hits e5 and opens the c1-bishop against g5, and after 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 the white queen hits the h8-rook; 4...Nf6 blocks the black queen's guard of g5, so 5.Bxg5 wins a pawn and pins the knight.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 e4.strategy: Advances the pawn to a square White attacks and Black cannot defend: 3.Nxe4 simply wins a pawn, and the extra space is gone.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight to guard e5 and watch d4, and keeps both an open and a closed set-up available. The cost is the c6 square: the knight takes the place of the c-pawn, so the plan of ...c6 and ...d5 is gone.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward e4 and d5 and keeps the other knight and the central break in reserve. Black gets central space with the e5-pawn, White the extra tempo and pressure along the long diagonal, so the game resembles a Sicilian with the colours reversed.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre before the bishop reaches g2. After cxd5 Qxd5 the queen hits the rook on h1 along the long diagonal, so White must block it with a developing move, but the early queen then loses time to Nc3. Black trades the d-pawn for White's c-pawn and pays with tempi.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, so that after cxd5 the c-pawn recaptures and Black keeps two pawns in the centre. The move develops no piece, so White uses the time to develop and work against the black centre.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop toward f2 and prepares castling. The set-up is sound, but the bishop can become a target for White's natural development, and White's long-diagonal bishop with a knight keeps an easy grip on d5.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, which supports e5 along the long diagonal, for a closed game. The move is sound but commits Black to this set-up early, while White, a tempo ahead, can start queenside play.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 d6.strategy: Supports e5 and frees the c8 bishop in a solid, waiting set-up. It concedes space and makes a later ...d5 cost another tempo, so White's long-diagonal bishop and queenside knight exert lasting pressure on d5.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly and prepares kingside castling. The move is sound but does nothing about the centre, and White builds a comfortable grip while Black still has to settle where the knights belong.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 for a Dutch-like attack with the e-pawn already on e5. It is a risky try rather than a refuted one: the h5-e8 diagonal and the e6 square are weakened, and White opens the centre with d4 and easy development.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 h5.name: English Opening: Drill Variation
1.c4 e5 2.g3 h5.strategy: Prepares ...h4 to undermine the g3 pawn and open the h-file against the fianchetto. White simply develops and keeps a slight edge, while the advanced pawn loosens Black's kingside. It is playable but a gamble.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Moves the knight to the rim, aiming at c5 and b4, but leaves e5 without support and the centre to White. ...Nc5 costs two moves and can be hit by b4.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5, but blocks the f8 bishop and the e7 square and invites Nc3-d5 with tempo on the queen. White develops while the queen has little to do.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qf6.strategy: Defends e5, but takes the best square from the king's knight, and Nc3-d5 later hits the queen with a gain of time. White develops while the queen has to move again.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qg5.strategy: Eyes d2 and g3, but both are well protected, and 3.h4 chases the queen away at once. Black loses time with the queen for nothing.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Bd6.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the d-pawn, which keeps the c8-bishop shut in. White develops and can take the centre at ease.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Bb4.strategy: Puts the bishop on b4, where it attacks nothing because d2 is guarded. A move such as a3 or Nc3 forces it to commit or retreat, gaining time for White.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes f5 and g4 but does nothing about d5 or the centre. ...Nf6 does the same job with central influence.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Ne7.strategy: Covers d5, but shuts in the f8-bishop, whose only diagonal runs through e7, so Black needs ...g6 or another knight move before castling.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that only takes b5 away from White's pieces. White develops without resistance.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and stops b4, but loses a tempo and weakens b5, where Nc3 can settle.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 b6.strategy: Aims for ...Bb7, but with Bg2 coming the bishop hangs on the long diagonal until something blocks it. A slow flank move that weakens c6 and leaves White ahead in development.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 c5.strategy: Mirrors the c-pawn and takes d4, but leaves d5 as a lasting hole that White's pieces can occupy and press on. Black has no easy way to challenge it.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 f6.strategy: Defends e5 but blocks the king's knight, weakens e6 and the king's diagonal, and ties Black to passive defence. White develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside and the long diagonal: after 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 the queen attacks the rook on h8 at once, and Black must block it. The kingside weaknesses stay for the rest of the game.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo to parry a threat that does not exist, because the c1 bishop is blocked by the d2 pawn. White simply develops.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 e4.strategy: Advances the pawn without support to a square that White will soon attack with pieces and a pawn. Black can hold it only by spending more time defending it while White develops.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qh4.strategy: Hangs the queen: the g3 pawn simply captures it with 3.gxh4.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good, blocks the f8 bishop and leaves the king in the centre for no reason. White develops and can open the position against the exposed king.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.bxa3 or 3.Nxa3 wins a piece for nothing.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn: 3.cxb5 wins it, and Black has no lead in development or open lines in return.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: The most natural reply: Black defends the pawn and develops a piece in one move, and the knight joins the fight for the centre. Black commits to nothing yet, so the set-up stays flexible. The price is that White keeps the initiative of the extra move and decides whether the game stays quiet or opens up.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Nimzowitsch-Flohr Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.background: Wikibooks' opening theory notes that 2.Nf3 can lead to a reversed Alekhine's Defence of sorts if Black replies ...e4. In his 2024 Modern Chess course on 1.c4 e5, Grandmaster Boris Avrukh describes the position after 3.Nd4 Nc6 as a reversed Alapin in which Black has not played ...c6, and calls 4.e3 White's main move and the speciality of Alexander Rakhmanov.
1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.strategy: Gains space and drives the knight from f3 at once; 3.Ng5 fails to 3...Qxg5, so the knight usually goes to the centre. The advanced pawn cramps White but also becomes a target that White can attack, so Black must keep supporting it. The game turns on whether that pawn holds or falls.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn and frees the c8-bishop, but the f8-bishop is hemmed in. The structure is solid and passive; White can strike in the centre at once or develop calmly.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the f8-bishop and puts the queen where 3.Nc3 and Nd5 hit it with gain of tempo. The pawn is not lost, but Black falls behind in development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6.strategy: Guards e5 with the queen but takes f6 from the knight and invites 3.Nc3 followed by Nd5 with gain of tempo. An early queen sortie that costs time without a clear purpose.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Bd6.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the d-pawn, so the c8-bishop stays shut in and ...d5 is hard to prepare. White develops freely and takes the centre while Black's pieces lack good squares; no material is lost.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Leaves e5 unprotected as a trap: after 3.Nxe5 Black sacrifices on f2 and the queen's checks win the knight back. But White keeps the bishop pair, and can also decline the trap and simply develop.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Strikes at c4 at once, but 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains a tempo on the queen and leaves White ahead in development, while 3.Nxe5 is also available.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn but takes f6 from the knight and weakens the e6-square and the e8-h5 diagonal. White gets an easy lead in development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Develops to the rim and heads for c5 or c7, but never guards e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the knight on a6 stays offside.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qg5.strategy: Eyes g2, but the queen steps onto a square the f3-knight covers: 3.Nxg5 wins it for nothing.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qh4.strategy: Puts the queen en prise to the f3-knight: 3.Nxh4 simply wins it.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Ke7.strategy: Forfeits castling and blocks the queen and the f8-bishop while e5 still hangs: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, with Black's king stuck in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Be7.strategy: Does not guard e5, which the f3-knight takes: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and the bishop cannot win it back.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the d2-pawn to the king but leaves e5 hanging: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and the pin does not win it back.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Ba3.strategy: Throws the bishop away: 3.Nxa3 or 3.bxa3 wins a piece for nothing, and e5 is still hanging.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Puts a knight on the rim where it does not help guard e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn and Black is left with a poorly placed piece.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops, but the knight does not guard e5 and there is no e4-pawn to win back: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn, and Black has open lines but no real compensation.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Ne7.strategy: Heads for g6 or c6 but does not guard e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the knight's journey does not win it back.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 but ignores the threat on e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the a-pawn move does nothing for development or the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space but leaves e5 en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the rook-pawn move plays no part in the fight for the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against the long diagonal but never defends e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the bishop on b7 meets only a solid g2-pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn on the flank while e5 also hangs: 3.cxb5 or 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn at once, and the b-pawn thrust has no follow-up in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 but leaves e5 undefended: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and ...Qa5 only hits the knight, which retreats with the extra pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Mirrors White's pawn but forgets e5: 3.Nxe5 takes it, and ...Nc6 trades the knight off while White keeps the extra pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Aims at space on the kingside but forgets the e5-pawn: 3.Nxe5 takes it, and a queen sortie to win it back only loses time.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto but leaves e5 en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and White can support the knight in the centre, so Black is simply a pawn down.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: A lunge that loosens the kingside for good and still leaves e5 hanging: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and the advanced g-pawn becomes a target.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that guards g5 but ignores the threat on e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the tempo contributes nothing to development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook-pawn for no reason and leaves e5 en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the h-pawn does nothing for the centre or development.
